catalog_quote: Lɛtɛ is a register tone language with two level tones, high and low tones, and the syllable functions as the tone-bearing unit. The following monosyllabic words are said with a high tone: (25). mɔ́ - 'this' nyɛ́ - 'go' nú - 'flesh/meat' bá - 'hand' The following monosyllabic words are said with a low tone: (26) kà - listen bɛ̀ - come gyì - eat yè - say The low and high tones may contrast as follows: (27) nù - drink nú - meat nyɔ̀ - switch on nyɔ́ - two bà - sew bá - hand/arms ... High and low tones may combine in words as follows: H- H L- H H- L L- L (28) hɛ́. !nɩ́ sò.kyí bó.bù Lɛ̀tɛ̀ 'scar' 'search for' 'bone' language/town A sequence of a high and a low tone on a syllable is perceived as a falling pitch (29a), whereas a low-high sequence on a syllable is perceived as a rising pitch (29b). It has however been observed that the rising pitch is rare in Lɛtɛ discourse. ... 5.1 Non-automatic downstep in Lɛtɛ When there is a sequence of two high tones occurring on two adjacent syllables, the second high tone is perceived at a slightly lower pitch than that of the first high tone (Figure 3). The second high tone is said to be downstepped (30). ... 4.2 Automatic downstep in Lɛtɛ This is caused by a cumulative effect of a local interaction between low and high tones. This results in a gradual lowering of pitch over a sentence or some unit; consequently, successive high tones are progressively lowered, often to a level phonetically below that of low tones earlier in the unit.
world_status: statement found in an open source

It has however been observed that the rising pitch is rare in Lɛtɛ discourse.' On printed p.32…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Leteh is described purely as a two-level (H, L) register tone language with the syllable as TBU, lexical and grammatical (tense/aspect) tone, HL/LH contours on single syllables, and automatic/non-automatic downstep; the author's dedicated phonology article and all her other opened descriptions never mention word stress or accent, so no stress placement statement exists in the accessible primary literature.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tonal notes only (rising LH contour rare; downstep of second of two adjacent H tones).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone illustrated on citation forms (monosyllabic minimal pairs, disyllables); downstep illustrated on sentences with pitch traces. Same characterisation repeated in Akrofi Ansah 2021 SAL 50(2) p.347 citing her 2009 Manchester PhD pp.65-66, and in JWAL 39(2) 2012.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe Leteh/Lɛtɛ as spoken in Larteh town (Akuapem, Eastern Region, Ghana) = Glottolog lart1238 / ISO lar; the author spells it Leteh, Lɛtɛ, Latɛ interchangeably. No dialect subdivision is described (single-town language). Related but distinct South Guang varieties already in the catalog (Gua/Anum guaa1238, Efutu awut1241) are not the same language.

tone_statements.citation: Akrofi Ansah, Mercy. 2022. Lɛtɛ verbal morphology and inflectional affixes. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies 18(2).
tone_statements.quote: The basic syllable structure of Lɛtɛ is CV, although syllabic nasals are also found in the language. Lɛtɛ is a tone language with two level tones: high and low. The lexical tone helps to distinguish meanings of words which otherwise are the same in terms of their constituents (3), whereas the grammatical tone, coupled with some verbal prefixes, is employed in making tense and aspectual distinctions (4). As examples in (3) and elsewhere in the paper demonstrate, the syllable is the tone-bearing unit in Lɛtɛ. (3) a. bà ‘sew’ bá ‘hand’ b. kù ‘cut’ kú ‘mountain’ c. bὲ ‘come’ bέ ‘proverb’
tone_statements.locator: p. 412, section 2 'Basic Typological features of Lɛtɛ', with ex. (3)
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones, high and low, the syllable the tone-bearing unit; lexical minimal pairs and grammatical tone for tense/aspect (past vs present by tone alone); H-L may surface as a fall on a CV stem.

The lexical tone is contrastive; it distinguishes meaning between two or more words which are the same morphologically. The grammatical tone distinguishes tense and aspectual forms, and also functions in category-changing derivational processes. Six verbal structures are identified in Lɛtɛ.
